hookLine: An engineer walked into the garage under the swimming pool, put a hammer to the ceiling, and wrote down what he heard.

captions.text: In October 2018, an engineer walked down into the garage under the swimming pool at
Champlain Towers South, put a hammer to the ceiling, and wrote down what he heard.
Two years and eight months later, at twenty-two minutes past one in the morning,
that building came down on the people asleep inside it.
Ninety-eight of them died.
What the engineer wrote is a public document.
So is the letter the board president sent her neighbours three years afterwards,
telling them the damage was getting worse and speeding up.
Everybody who could have acted had been told.
Twice.
In writing.
And there is a third document, published this June, five years late.
It says that by the night the building fell, it had already been falling for three
weeks.
Surfside, Florida.
This is a film about five documents.
Two of them were warnings, one was a set of minutes, one was a drawing nobody looked
at for forty years, and the last one arrived five years too late to be of use to
anybody.
Champlain Towers South was built in 1981 and stood twelve storeys above the sand on
Florida's Atlantic coast.
A hundred and thirty-six apartments, a lobby, a lift, a corridor of identical doors.
From the beach it looked like every other building on that stretch of coast, because
it was.
Behind it, at ground level, there was a swimming pool.
That pool sat on a slab of concrete.
Under the slab there was a garage.
Everything that follows happens in the space between those two sentences.
Above the slab: water, tiles, loungers, planters full of heavy tropical greenery.
Below it: columns, painted bays, and the cars belonging to the people upstairs.
The deck was a roof, and almost nobody who walked on it had reason to think of it
that way.
A deck like that is a flat plate.
No beams.
The floor is a single flat sheet of concrete and the columns push straight up into
its underside.
Where a column arrives there is usually a thickened square of slab, a drop panel,
because that patch of concrete has to take everything the column takes.
There are hundreds of thousands of garages built exactly like it, all over the
world, and nearly all of them will stand for as long as anyone needs them to.
What makes the type unforgiving is where its strength lives.
Load in a flat plate does not spread out.
It runs to the columns and crowds around them, so the strength of a whole floor is
decided in the few square metres of concrete at each column head.
Engineers give those patches a surplus.
The connection is built to hold considerably more than anyone expects to put on it,
because a building gets fifty years of things nobody predicted.
That surplus has a name — the margin against failure — and it is the difference
between a structure that survives its own surprises and one that does not.
So the object at the centre of this story is not a tower.
It is a joint, repeated thirty or forty times in the dark, under a swimming pool.
And a joint of that kind gives almost nothing away.
It is at the top of a column, in a car park, above head height, in poor light,
behind a layer of concrete whose whole purpose is to cover what matters.
For thirty-seven years those joints did their work and nobody had cause to think
about them.
People bought apartments there for the reasons people buy apartments on that coast.
You could hear the water from the balcony.
The deck caught the sun before the street did.
Cars went down the ramp and came back up, several times a day, for four decades.
One more thing about that building, and it decides everything that happens in the
second half of this story.
The people in it were owners.
Not tenants.
There was no landlord upstairs to write to when something went wrong, and no company
that owned the structure and rented out the rooms.
A condominium is a building owned in pieces by the people living in it, and the
parts nobody lives in — the roof, the columns, the garage, the deck under the
swimming pool — are owned by all of them together.
Which means that when the concrete holding up that pool needed work, there was
nobody to ask.
There was only each other.
And of everything held in common, the deck was the piece people actually used.
A corridor is somewhere you pass through.
A garage is where the car goes.
The deck was the reason to live there — the pool, the loungers, the sun in the
morning, the one part of that address a resident would show a visitor.
It was also the roof of the garage, and the only surface in the building where the
thing everybody enjoyed and the thing holding it up were the same slab of concrete.
For thirty-seven years, nobody had to look.
Then the building turned forty, and Florida stopped leaving it alone.
A building of that age on that coast has to be recertified.
It is not a request and it is not triggered by anything anyone notices — it is
triggered by the calendar.
Whatever was under that pool had been under it since 1981, unexamined and
unmeasured, and now somebody was going to have to go down there with a light and put
a number on it.
In 2018 the association hired somebody to do exactly that.
His name was Frank Morabito.
His firm had been asked for a structural field survey — the kind of report a
building of that age on that coast needs before it is recertified.
What that word covers matters here, because it is the only reason anyone was down
there.
Recertification is not an inspection of the kind that happens when somebody
complains.
It is a scheduled reckoning, imposed from outside, in which a building has to
demonstrate that it is still what it was certified to be.
Somebody qualified goes over the structure and the electrical systems and writes
down what they find, and the findings go to the municipality.
Which means the report Morabito was writing was never going to be a private
document.
It was going to have two readers: the people who owned the building, and the town.
The work is more physical than the phrase suggests.
He walked the deck.
He went down the ramp into the garage.
And he did the thing that tells you most about concrete, which is to hit it.
Sound concrete rings.
Concrete that has come away from the steel inside it gives back a flat, dead knock,
because there is a void behind the surface where the two used to be joined.
A man with a hammer and a trained ear can map a defect through a wall that looks
perfectly good, and he can do it faster than any instrument, and for the price of an
afternoon.
It is the oldest test there is, and on a coast it is the one that matters, because
the failure that kills a slab of this kind happens behind a surface that stays
smooth right up until the end.
Here is what that dead knock means, because the whole of what happened later is in
it.
Concrete is not solid the way a stone is.
It is a hard sponge, threaded with pores.
Inside it there is steel, and the steel is what actually holds a floor up — the
concrete's job is to grip it and to keep water away from it.
In a healthy slab the chemistry of the cement keeps that steel passive, coated in a
film a few molecules thick that stops it rusting at all.
Salt destroys the film.
On an ocean front, salt arrives in spray, lands on a deck, sits in whatever water
does not drain, and works down through the pores until it reaches the bar.
Then the steel begins to corrode, and corroding steel does something ordinary rust
on a gate does not do.
It swells.
Rust takes up several times the volume of the metal it came from, and it does that
inside a material with nowhere to give.
The concrete splits outward from the bar.
The split lets in more water.
More steel corrodes.
More concrete splits.
The process feeds itself, it speeds up, and the surface gives nothing away until
late.
That is what Morabito was listening for.
He found it in three places, and he named them: the pool deck, the entrance drive,
and the planters.
Take them in order, because each one is a different version of the same failure.
The pool deck is the largest and the most important, and it is where the
waterproofing had gone.
A deck like that is built to shed rain within minutes.
When it does not — when the falls are too shallow, or an outlet sits proud of the
surface, or a seam has lifted a millimetre — the water does not leave.
It stands.
And the waterproof layer is the only thing between a puddle that sits there for two
days and the steel underneath.
The entrance drive is the same construction doing a harder job, because cars drive
over it.
Every vehicle coming down that ramp is a load put on and taken off again, thousands
of times a year, working at whatever cracks are already there.
The planters are the quiet one.
A planter is a box of wet soil.
It is heavy when it is dry and heavier every time it rains, it sits in exactly the
same place for decades, and the water in it has to go somewhere.
Put one on a waterproofed deck and you have made a permanent damp patch on a surface
designed to stay dry, directly above the structure.
Morabito wrote down all three, in October 2018.
He also found the reason.
The waterproofing under the pool deck had failed — not was failing, had failed — so
water had been reaching the structure below for a long time.
In his report he wrote that the failed waterproofing was "causing major structural
damage to the concrete structural slab below these areas."
Major, in an engineer's writing, is not decoration.
It is a category.
Structural separates damage to the thing holding the building up from damage to
everything else.
He described the concrete itself as showing "abundant concrete cracking and
spalling."
Spalling is what it sounds like: concrete coming off in pieces, pushed away from
behind by steel that has swollen.
On the underside of a slab it is the visible end of a process that has been running
invisibly for years, above reinforcement no longer the size the drawings called for.
Consider the position he was writing from.
A structural field survey is addressed to the people who own the building — and they
are the people who will have to pay for whatever it says.
An engineer who overstates costs his clients money they did not need to spend.
An engineer who understates leaves them standing under it.
There is only one way out of that, which is to write down what is there and price it
honestly, and let the people who own the building decide.
Then he did what engineering reports do.
He priced it.
Nine point one million dollars.
For a building of a hundred and thirty-six apartments that is an average of about
sixty-seven thousand a household.
Shares follow the size of the apartment, so some owners would have owed rather less
and some a great deal more.
The report went to the association, where it became one board's problem.
And then somebody on that board did something about it.
Two days before the November 2018 meeting, a board member named Mara Chouela took
the report — along with a second one on the mechanical and electrical systems — and
sent it out of the association, to the town of Surfside.
That is a small act and it is the largest one in this story.
Nothing obliged her to do it.
A report commissioned by an association belongs to the association; forwarding it to
the municipality invites the municipality in.
She sent it anyway, and she sent it before the meeting rather than after, which is
the difference between telling somebody and asking them to come.
It is the only moment in the whole record where a named individual, holding this
information, moves it towards somebody with the power to act on it.
It reached Ross Prieto, the town's chief building official — the office that decides
what a building is allowed to be.
It issues permits, it signs off inspections, and when it says nothing needs doing,
nothing does.
He came to the board meeting.
There is only one room in this story, and this is it.
A condominium board meeting on a weeknight.
Folding chairs.
A jug of water.
Seven or eight people on the board and a scattering of residents who came.
Somewhere on that table, two days old, is a report saying that the slab under their
swimming pool has major structural damage and that repairing it will cost nine point
one million dollars.
The town's building official is there.
According to the minutes, he told them the building was in very good shape.
That is what the record says he said.
It is written in the association's own minutes, taken by the association's own
secretary, in the ordinary course of an evening's business.
Six words.
In very good shape.
They were said in a room where the report was already sitting on the table.
Not a summary of the report, not a rumour of it — the document itself, forty-eight
hours old, forwarded to his office by a member of that board.
The engineer's finding and the official's reassurance were in the same room on the
same evening, and only one of them was spoken aloud.
Set that against what had happened forty-eight hours earlier.
A member of that board had taken the report out of the association and carried it to
the town, before the meeting, so that the town would be in the room holding it.
The town came, holding it, and said the building was in very good shape.
Those are the two human acts in this story, and they cancel each other out.
One person moved the information towards authority.
Authority handed it back as reassurance.
Nobody shouted, nobody was overruled, and nothing in the minutes records a
disagreement — which is exactly why it worked.
And a sentence like that does what sentences like that do.
It forbade nothing.
It ordered nothing.
It started no clock.
A board holding a report about major structural damage was told by the authority on
buildings that theirs was fine, and after that the repair stopped being an
obligation and became a project — a very large bill that a few hundred neighbours
would have to agree among themselves to pay, on a timetable of their own choosing,
with nobody waiting at the other end of it.
The work did not begin.
The report went into the association's files and the town's files, and stayed there.
A document that is filed is a document that is no longer moving.
Nobody has to read it again.
Nobody is required to act on it.
It goes on being true, in a drawer, at the exact rate the concrete goes on getting
worse.
In June 2021, after the building came down, a reporter reached Prieto and asked
about it.
He said he did not remember receiving the report.
On a lawyer's advice, he declined to say more.
That is the entire record of that exchange.
What he read, what he understood, what he meant — none of it is established.
What is established is the sequence.
The report was written.
It was delivered to two institutions.
It was read into a meeting as good news.
And under the swimming pool, the concrete went on doing what concrete does.
Then almost three years pass, and the reason is not engineering.
There are two ways to find that money.
Save it in advance, in a reserve, which means charging everybody more every month
for decades against a repair nobody can see yet.
Or raise a special assessment when the bill lands, which means asking several
hundred people at once for tens of thousands of dollars each.
At the start of 2021, the reserve fund at Champlain Towers South held about seven
hundred and six thousand dollars.
A study of what a building like that ought to have set aside put the figure at
around ten point three million.
Put the two next to each other.
Seven hundred and six thousand.
Ten point three million.
Seven per cent.
That is what forty years of monthly contributions had put in the account against the
work the building was going to need — and the shortfall was not an accident or a
theft.
It was a series of ordinary, popular decisions, taken one year at a time, by people
who were charging themselves.
So the second route is the ordinary one, and it moves at the speed of persuasion.
And persuasion, in a condominium, is a strange currency.
Every owner has a vote and a bill, and the two arrive together.
Saying yes means writing a cheque for something invisible.
Saying no costs nothing today, and the thing you are refusing to pay for makes no
complaint.
There is no meter running where anyone can see it.
A board can put the engineer's report in front of every owner — and this one did —
and it will still be a document about concrete, addressed to people who are being
asked for money.
The report is the evidence and the invoice at the same time, and evidence that comes
attached to a price is heard differently from evidence that does not.
Estimates age while it moves.
Construction costs climb, and corroding steel does not pause for a vote — every
month of discussion is another month of the same process running underneath the
discussion.
By early 2021 the work had been repriced.
By early 2021 the figure had been settled at fifteen million dollars, and
apportioned by apartment.
The range is what to hear.
The owner of a one-bedroom would pay eighty thousand, one hundred and ninety
dollars.
The owner of the four-bedroom penthouse would pay three hundred and thirty-six
thousand, one hundred and thirty-five.
You could pay it in one sum, or monthly across fifteen years.
Two and a half years had turned nine point one million into fifteen.
Some of that is simply what building work costs after two and a half years.
Some of it is scope — the longer a repair waits, the more of the structure it has to
include, because the damage does not hold still while the money is discussed.
A crack that needed sealing in 2018 needs cutting out and rebuilding later.
That is the ordinary tax on delay, and it is the reason the number in a structural
report is a perishable number.
The estimate was not wrong.
It had simply expired.
That was the sum an owner had to find.
Not for a new lobby or a better pool — for concrete under a deck, most of it in a
garage, none of it visible from any apartment in the building.
Delay was expensive in a way nobody could see and cheap in a way everybody could
feel.
That is the most reliable way there is for a decision to be postponed.
An owner in that building in 2019 was being asked to believe three things at once.
That there was something seriously wrong with the structure.
That it would cost them tens of thousands of dollars.
And that the town's own chief building official had stood in their board meeting and
said the place was in very good shape.
Any two of those are manageable.
All three at once is a very good reason to wait for more information.
And then, after three years, they voted for it.
In April 2021 the association approved the assessment — fifteen million dollars,
ahead of the building's forty-year recertification.
Three years of estimates and meetings and elections ended in a decision to raise the
money and do the work.
Every household in that building now knew exactly what its share came to, and when
it was due.
To explain the decision, the board president, Jean Wodnicki, wrote to the residents
on the ninth of April.
It is the plainest document in this story, and it was written to be persuasive,
because it had to be.
That letter is the second warning, and the harder of the two to read, because a
consultant did not write it.
A neighbour wrote it, to neighbours, about their own home, while asking them for
money.
She told them what had happened since the engineer's visit.
The observable damage, including in the garage, "has gotten significantly worse
since the initial inspection."
She told them it was "accelerating."
And she told them where that led: the damage would "begin to multiply exponentially"
in the years ahead.
Read the sequence, because it is short.
October 2018: an engineer writes that the slab under the pool deck has major
structural damage.
April 2021: the president of the board writes to every resident that it has got
significantly worse, that it is speeding up, and that it is going to multiply.
Nobody in that building was uninformed.
And the money had been voted.
There was a date on it.
Owners had until the first of July to pay the sum in full or commit to the
fifteen-year plan.
Then people went on living there.
There is nothing to report from April, May and the first three weeks of June except
ordinary life in a building where the paperwork had finally started to move.
The damage had been surveyed.
The work had a price.
The money had been voted, and the first of July was coming.
This is the answer to the question people ask afterwards, which is why nobody left.
Nobody left because there was nothing to leave.
A building with a repair project is not an emergency; it is the most ordinary
situation on that coast.
Scaffolding goes up somewhere along that shoreline every week of the year.
An owner who had read every word of the April letter would have concluded,
correctly, that their building needed expensive work and that the board now had the
money to do it.
The damage was also in the two places in a residential building that nobody looks
at: the garage, and the underside of a deck.
Nothing in an apartment on the ninth floor was different in June 2021 from how it
had been in 2015.
So the spring passed the way springs pass.
Cars went down the ramp and parked under the slab that two people had now put in
writing.
Towels were left on loungers.
After heavy rain, water stood in a shallow sheet across the deck the way it had for
years, and then went, the way it always had.
The repairs were being organised.
That is the thing to hold on to about those weeks, because it is what makes them
ordinary rather than ominous.
A building that had argued with itself for three years had stopped arguing.
There was a report, a price, a vote, and a date.
The residents of Champlain Towers South had every reason to believe that the worst
part of this was going to be the bill.
The building came down on the twenty-fourth of June.
The money was due on the first of July.
Seven days.
Nobody in that building ever paid the assessment.
Nobody was waiting for anything to happen.
They were waiting for work to start.
And in the first week of June, in the garage nobody had any reason to be standing
in, two connections between the columns and the pool deck slab failed.
There was nothing to hear.
Nothing shifted that anyone would notice from the ninth floor.
A connection that had been carrying its share of that deck stopped carrying it, and
the load went into the concrete and the columns beside it — because load does not
stop existing when a support does.
It has to go somewhere, and it goes to whatever is nearest.
Nobody was told, because nobody knew.
The people who could have been told were upstairs, waiting for the first of July.
And here is the part that separates this from every warning that had been written
down.
The two documents in this story describe deterioration — waterproofing that has
failed, concrete cracking, steel corroding, damage getting worse.
All of that is a condition.
It is measured in years, it is repaired on a schedule, and it is what an assessment
is for.
What began in the first week of June was not a condition.
It was a sequence.
One connection handing its load to the next, then that one handing it on.
Nobody in that building had been told to watch for a sequence, because nobody knew
there was one.
The repairs being arranged that month were the right repairs for the problem in the
reports, and the problem in the reports had, that month, quietly become a different
problem.
For five years nobody could say that with authority.
There were theories, and some of them were good, and none of them was a finding.
On the twenty-second of June 2026, the National Institute of Standards and
Technology published the technical findings of its investigation — the National
Construction Safety Team, co-led by Judith Mitrani-Reiser and Glenn Bell, five years
of collecting the physical evidence, modelling the structure, and testing what the
drawings said against what had actually been poured.
They did not reach that on paper.
The team worked through about two dozen ways the failure could have started — a
sinkhole under the site, a failed pile, the ground-floor slab tearing away from the
basement wall — and to test the one rival that mattered, they built replicas of the
garage columns and loaded them until they broke.
Those columns failed brittle and all at once.
That is not what this building did.
So it was not the columns.
Two connections between garage columns and the pool deck failed in early June 2021.
And the failure did not stop where it started.
It spread — connection by connection, over about three weeks, until the
twenty-fourth of June.
The mechanism has a name.
Punching shear: the characteristic failure of a flat plate, and the exact risk that
the thickened patch of concrete at every column head exists to prevent.
The column stays where it is.
The slab, loaded from above, comes down around it.
All the load in that bay is trying to get into that one column, so the concrete
immediately around the column head is in the most punishing condition anywhere in
the floor.
When it goes, it does not crack politely across the middle of the room.
A cone of concrete shears out around the column and the head passes through the
slab, the way a pencil goes through paper.
Then the load that connection was carrying transfers to the connections beside it —
which were built to carry their own share and not somebody else's.
If they have surplus, they hold, and the building stands there with an injury nobody
can see.
If they do not, the next one goes.
That is why the number in the finding is three weeks and not three seconds.
A structure that fails all at once gives nobody an interval.
This deck failed in instalments, and each one left the survivors carrying more.
It ran like that for three weeks, under a swimming pool, above a garage with cars
parked in it.
What the finding gives is two dates and a process.
Two connections, first week of June.
The whole thing down on the twenty-fourth.
Between them, three weeks of a structure handing its load from one place to the
next.
There is no photograph of that.
No witness.
No alarm, no reading, no gauge.
No moment in those three weeks that anybody recorded, because the only place it was
happening was above the cars, in the dark, behind concrete.
The building stood.
That is all anybody can say about the middle of it.
It stood on the fifth of June.
It stood on the twelfth.
It stood on the nineteenth.
It stood while the people inside it decided whether to pay eighty thousand dollars
in one sum or across fifteen years.
Nothing in the record shows anybody knew it had started.
Which leaves the question that has been open since the first minute.
Why was there no surplus left?
The answer comes in two parts, and the second is worse.
The first part is the deck.
Its structural design was understrength.
The steel reinforcement in it had been misplaced during construction — not where the
drawings put it.
Over the decades it had been given more to carry than it began with: heavy planters,
added sand, pavers.
And the steel inside it had been corroding the whole time, in a place where water
stood.
Now put two documents side by side.
October 2018: an engineer writes that failed waterproofing is causing major
structural damage to the slab below the pool deck, the entrance drive and the
planters.
June 2026: a federal investigation finds that the collapse began at two connections
under the pool deck; that the deck was understrength; that its reinforcement was in
the wrong place; that heavy planters, added sand and pavers had increased its load;
and that its steel had been corroding for decades.
One man with a hammer and a national laboratory with five years of modelling ended
up pointing at the same tubs of soil.
The second part of the answer is one sentence, and it is not about the pool deck at
all.
Judith Mitrani-Reiser: "When building structures are designed and built to required
codes and standards, they have margins against failure, meaning they should be able
to support much more load than they are expected to bear.
In the case of Champlain Towers South, however, these margins against failure were
too narrow from the start."
From the start.
Not from 2018, when the survey was written.
Not from 2021, when the assessment passed.
From the beginning of the building's life, before anyone in this story had moved in,
the distance between what that structure could carry and what it would be asked to
carry was thinner than a building is supposed to have.
Every argument in that association about money — every meeting, every vote, every
owner who could not afford it and every owner who could — was an argument about
restoring something to a condition it had never been in.
The 2018 report is not diminished by that.
What it described was real, and it was getting worse, and it needed the money it
said it needed.
But it was a report about a building's deterioration, written on the assumption
every such report makes: that there was a sound structure underneath the damage, and
that repairing the damage would return it to that.
The federal finding is that there was no such condition to return to.
Glenn Bell, the other co-lead, said where the shortfall came from: "The low margins
against failure were primarily caused by two factors… First, severe and widespread
deviations in the building's original structural design from the codes and standards
of the day, but also some limitations in those codes and standards.
And second, deviations in the building's construction from the design drawings."
Two gaps.
Between the code and the design.
Between the design and the building that was actually poured.
Reinforcement in the wrong position disappears the moment the concrete goes in —
entombed there, wrong for the life of the structure, and nothing anybody does
afterwards will move it.
The finding is that this building had both.
Neither is visible to a resident.
Neither can be found by walking a garage with a hammer, because a hammer tells you
the state of the concrete, not whether the drawing it was built from was ever good
enough.
And neither is fixed by approving an assessment.
On the twenty-fourth of June 2021, at twenty-two minutes past one in the morning,
Champlain Towers South came down.
It was a Thursday.
Most of the people inside were asleep.
The building was forty years old.
The failure inside it was three weeks old.
There was no storm.
No earthquake.
No impact, no fire, no explosion.
And it did not come down all at once.
The pool deck went first.
The tower stood for more than four minutes after that.
Then the columns low in the east wing let go, and the rest of it followed them down.
Four minutes is long enough to put shoes on.
Nobody did, because nothing in that building existed to tell anybody that the first
part of it had already gone.
By then the two connections that failed in the first week of June had been handing
their load on for three weeks, and every transfer had made the next one likelier
than the one before it.
The federal finding does not describe a building that was struck by anything, or
shaken, or overloaded from outside.
It describes a structure that ran out of places to put the weight.
Ninety-eight of them died.
This film will not describe that, or name them, or stage their last minutes, or show
the search.
Their families have been asked to look at those pictures for five years.
What the record holds is this.
The building had been examined, written about, priced, argued over and warned about
— by an engineer, and then by one of its own residents.
The cost of repairing it had been counted twice.
And when it went, it went in the middle of the night, without notice, out of a
garage nobody was standing in.
The record is clear about what those three weeks did not include.
There was no evacuation order, because nobody had grounds to give one.
There was no inspection in progress.
There was no warning to the residents that anything had changed, because as far as
anyone knew nothing had.
The failure that had started in the first week of June was in the one part of the
building that produces no symptoms upstairs — no cracked plaster, no jammed door, no
sound.
The people who went to bed that night were living in a building that had been
diagnosed, priced and scheduled for repair.
That was the true position, and it was also, by then, three weeks out of date.
On the twenty-third of June 2022, the day before the first anniversary, Judge
Michael Hanzman of the Miami-Dade Circuit Court gave final approval to the
settlement of the claims.
More than twenty-four defendants.
One billion, twenty-one million, one hundred and ninety-nine thousand dollars.
Nine point one million to repair it in 2018.
Fifteen million by 2021.
One billion and twenty-one million afterwards.
About ninety-six million of that was set aside for the people who lost one of the
hundred and thirty-six apartments.
Judge Hanzman, from the bench: "It will never be enough to compensate them for the
tragic loss they have suffered.
This settlement is the best we can do.
It's a remarkable result.
It is extraordinary."
In December 2021 a Miami-Dade grand jury reported on the collapse, six months after
it happened.
It recommended inspections and reserve funds and the other things this case had made
obvious to everybody who read about it.
It did not reach a conclusion about what had caused this building to fall.
Nobody could say it yet.
The answer was four and a half years away, in a federal laboratory, in a report that
landed long after the settlement was paid, the site was cleared, and the story had
stopped being news.
No individual and no company has been criminally charged.
Nobody has been charged for the design.
Nobody has been charged for what was poured.
Nobody has been charged for the three years, or for the six words in the minutes, or
for the seven per cent in the reserve account.
There is no defendant, because there is no single act — and the law, on the whole,
punishes acts.
Almost everything that mattered at Champlain Towers South was written down before it
happened.
The waterproofing had failed: October 2018.
The damage was major and structural: October 2018.
It was significantly worse, and accelerating: April 2021.
The price of stopping it, twice — and both times smaller than the price of not
stopping it.
One thing was not written down anywhere a resident could read it, and it was the
thing that decided the outcome.
The margins had been too narrow since 1981.
That was in the drawings, and in what was poured instead of the drawings, and nobody
read either until a federal laboratory did it in the year 2026.
So the arguments in that building were real arguments about a real problem,
conducted honestly, and aimed at the wrong forty years.
The residents were trying to repair a building that had been failing since it was
finished.
What they were assessing themselves fifteen million dollars to restore was a
condition it had never been in.
The building did not fall because nobody knew.
It fell with the paperwork in order.
